title: Jean Louise Finch
text: In my [memmories|memories|Spell 'memories' with one m after 'me': memories.], Maycomb is full of summer light. I can still [saw|see|After 'can', use the base verb: see.] the white houses and the trees beside the road. People sit outside after supper and talk across their gardens. A dog [bark|barks|'A dog' is singular, so use 'barks'.]. Someone calls a child home. I remember [that|those|Use 'those' with the plural noun 'sounds'.] small sounds better than the names above the shops. They make the town feel close again.

title: Jean Louise Finch
text: Whenever I think of Maycomb, I hear a screen door closing. Clap! Then comes the soft noise of evening talk, drifting between the porches. Our street seemed endless when I [were|was|Use 'was' with 'I' when describing the past: I was small.] small, although I could walk its length in [minuts|minutes|The correct spelling is 'minutes'.]. I remember women carrying shopping bags and men resting under trees. [There|Their|'Their' shows that the movements belong to the people.] ordinary movements [given|gave|Use the simple past 'gave' as the main verb here; 'given' needs an auxiliary.] shape to my childhood world.

title: Jean Louise Finch
text: Distance has sharpened certain details of Maycomb: a grocer [fold|folding|Use the -ing form in this descriptive phrase: a grocer folding paper.] paper around a purchase, porch shadows lengthening across the steps, the squeak of a reluctant gate. Whole streets have blurred, yet these small movements [remain,|remain.|End this complete sentence with a full stop before the next sentence begins.] As a child, I thought the town contained everything worth knowing. Now I remember how confidently its inhabitants [meassured|measured|The correct spelling is 'measured', with one s.] the world without [leave|leaving|After the preposition 'without', use the -ing form: without leaving.] their own front yards.

title: Scout
text: The best bit of Maycomb is the road outside our house. [There is|There are|Use 'there are' before the plural noun 'trees'.] trees to climb and plenty of room to run. In summer, the [duzt|dust|The correct spelling is 'dust'.] gets between my toes. I [doesn't|don't|Use 'don't' with 'I': I don't mind.] mind. Grown people sit on their porches and tell us to [slowed|slow|After 'to', use the base verb in 'to slow down'.] down, but they never go anywhere fast. Even the dogs sleep through most of the afternoon.

title: Scout
text: By lunchtime, the street is hot [enogh|enough|The correct spelling is 'enough'.] to make me [hops|hop|After 'make me', use the base verb: make me hop.] across it. I like the shady places best, especially where tree roots push up like knuckles. You can find beetles there if nobody calls you inside. Maycomb has too many people asking where I'm going. How can I tell [they|them|After the verb 'tell', use the object pronoun 'them'.]? Sometimes I haven't [decide|decided|After 'haven't', use the past participle: haven't decided.] until I get there.

title: Scout
text: From the courthouse steps, I can see hats bobbing through the square, each with a grown person underneath who [think|thinks|'Who' refers to 'a grown person', so the verb is singular: thinks.] they're [terrible|terribly|Use the adverb 'terribly' to modify the adjective 'important'.] important. Down at street level, there's better stuff: ants dragging crumbs, a loose board that [claterrs|clatters|The correct spelling is 'clatters', with double t.] when I jump on it, dogs with business of [there|their|Use the possessive 'their' in 'business of their own'.] own. Adults complain that nothing happens here. I reckon they're looking too high up.

title: Jem
text: I know most of the [streats|streets|The correct spelling is 'streets', with ee.] in Maycomb, and I like [show|showing|Use 'like showing' or 'like to show', not 'like show'.] the younger children around. Beyond the houses, [there is|there are|Use 'there are' with the plural noun 'fields'.] fields and long roads. I'd like to follow them one day. For now, I watch the cars coming through the square. Their wheels make little clouds of dust, and I try to guess how far they've [travel|travelled|After 'they've', use a past participle: they've travelled.].

title: Jem
text: Saturday brings the farmers into town, and I like watching them [parks|park|After 'watching them', the verb can be the base form: watching them park.] their wagons near the shops. Their [boot's|boots|Use the plural 'boots'; an apostrophe is not needed.] carry red earth onto the pavement. I've started [notice|noticing|After 'started', use an -ing form or a to-infinitive: started noticing.] things like that: who has work, who buys very little, who walks home. Maycomb used to feel like one big playground. These days, I sometimes wonder what keeps the grown people so [worryed|worried|Change y to i before -ed: worried.].

title: Jem
text: A wagon wheel rattles over the uneven road, [scatter|scattering|Use the -ing form to add an action to the main clause: scattering the dogs.] the dogs outside the store. I watch the driver [counts|count|After 'watch the driver', use the base form or an -ing form, not 'counts'.] his money twice before going in. Once, I'd have been [intrested|interested|The correct spelling is 'interested': inter-ested.] only in the horses. Lately, the town keeps showing me things I hadn't thought to notice: patched sleeves, tired shoulders, the careful way some men ask a price before [touch|touching|After the preposition 'before', use an -ing form: before touching.] anything.

title: Atticus Finch
text: [Befor|Before|The correct spelling is 'Before', including the final e.] work, I enjoy the walk into town. The shops are opening, and people stop to say good morning. Some look tired, even early in the day. I try to [listening|listen|After 'try to', use the base verb: try to listen.] when they speak. Each house [have|has|'Each house' is singular, so use 'has'.] a family with its own worries. Maycomb is small enough for me to know [much|many|Use 'many' with countable plural nouns: many names.] names, but names don't tell me everything.

title: Atticus Finch
text: There's usually someone [wait|waiting|Use an -ing form after 'someone' to describe what the person is doing: someone waiting.] to speak to me before I reach my office. A farmer with his hat in his hands; a neighbour concerned about a fence. I don't hurry [they|them|Use the object pronoun 'them' after 'hurry'.]. In a town this small, [peoples|people's|Use the possessive 'people's' to show whose troubles they are.] troubles travel the same streets as their shopping. By evening, I welcome the [quite|quiet|'Quiet' means peace or little noise. 'Quite' is a different word.] of my porch and the sound of my children nearby.

title: Atticus Finch
text: On my morning walk, the square gradually fills with voices: shopkeepers exchanging news, farmers discussing weather, someone questioning a bill. Familiar conversations, though the [anxeity|anxiety|The correct spelling is 'anxiety': anx-i-ety.] beneath them deserves [attention,|attention.|These are separate complete sentences; use a full stop here.] A failed crop can enter a household long before it enters an account book. I know these streets well enough to greet [there|their|'Their' refers to the streets and shows that the occupants belong there.] occupants; understanding what burdens each person [require|requires|The subject is the -ing clause 'understanding what burdens each person', which takes singular 'requires'.] rather more patience.

title: Calpurnia
text: My day begins before the children are [awaik|awake|The correct spelling is 'awake'.]. Outside, Maycomb is quiet, but the kitchen soon fills with noise. Clink! A spoon falls against a [pans|pan|After 'a', use a singular countable noun: a pan.], and somebody wants breakfast. Later, I walk past houses where other [women is|women are|'Women' is plural, so use 'are'.] already working. On Sunday, I see friends at church. We talk, sing and share what we [cans|can|Modal verbs do not take -s: we can.]. Those voices stay with me all week.

title: Calpurnia
text: While the town is still [rubing|rubbing|Double the final b before adding -ing: rubbing.] sleep from [it's|its|'Its' is possessive. 'It's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.] eyes, I've got breakfast to prepare. Soon there'll [is|be|After 'will', including the contraction 'there'll', use the base form 'be'.] footsteps on the stairs and questions from the kitchen door. My working day follows the Finch family's needs, but Maycomb holds my own friends and family too. At church, familiar voices rise around me, and for a while [nobody are|nobody is|'Nobody' takes a singular verb: nobody is.] calling for their supper.

title: Calpurnia
text: A kitchen window gives you a different view of Maycomb. While visitors admire tidy porches, I notice the hands that [scrubs|scrub|'That' refers to the plural noun 'hands', so use 'scrub'.] the steps and carry the washing. Work leaves its marks everywhere, if you care to look. On Sundays, [amoung|among|The correct spelling is 'among'; do not add u.] my own congregation, I can set those household demands [aside,|aside.|Use a full stop to separate these complete sentences.] The singing reaches me before I've [find|found|After 'I've', use the past participle 'found': I've found my place.] my place, warm with familiar voices.

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Out in my [gardin|garden|The correct spelling is 'garden'.], I can hear half the street. [Children runs|Children run|'Children' is plural, so use 'run'.] past the gate, and someone always stops for a chat. I like [a few company|a little company|'Company' means companionship here and is uncountable: a little company.] while I work. The flowers need water in this heat, and so do I. By late afternoon, my hands are brown with earth. I wash them, then go inside to make something [sweetly|sweet|Use an adjective after 'something': something sweet.].

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Rain has a lovely way of [change|changing|After the preposition 'of', use the -ing form: a way of changing.] Maycomb. The dusty [leafs|leaves|The plural of the plant noun 'leaf' is 'leaves'.] shine, the earth smells fresh, and all my neighbours discover urgent [resons|reasons|The correct spelling is 'reasons'.] to stay indoors. I pull on my gardening gloves and enjoy the peace. Afterwards, a few children may appear at the gate. There's generally cake in my kitchen, provided they can [waits|wait|After 'can', use the base verb: can wait.] while I finish with these weeds.

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Give Maycomb a patch of bare earth and somebody will pronounce it [hopelessly|hopeless|Use an adjective to describe 'it' after 'pronounce': pronounce it hopeless.]. I prefer to [fetching|fetch|After 'prefer to', use the base verb: prefer to fetch.] a spade. Even in this heat, there's pleasure in coaxing colour from [stuborn|stubborn|The correct spelling is 'stubborn', with double b.] soil while bees bustle between the flowers. By afternoon, neighbours lean over my fence with advice I haven't [request|requested|After 'haven't', use the past participle: haven't requested.]. I let them talk, pinch away a dead bloom, and carry on planting.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: You can learn a lot from [mine|my|Use 'my' before a noun: my front porch. 'Mine' stands alone.] front porch. The shops are close, so [neerly|nearly|The correct spelling is 'nearly'.] everyone [walk|walks|'Everyone' takes a singular verb: everyone walks.] past my house. I notice new hats, dirty shoes and people who look upset. Sometimes I call [they|them|Use the object pronoun 'them' in 'call them over'.] over for a talk. It's good to know your neighbours. Besides, if a strange car stops in our street, somebody should find out why.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: Well, there goes another [visitors|visitor|'Another' takes a singular countable noun here: another visitor.] to the house across the street. A cousin, perhaps, although nobody [mention|mentioned|'Yesterday' places this action in the past: mentioned.] a cousin yesterday. From my porch, I keep an eye on these things. Maycomb looks quiet to strangers, but [thats|that's|The contraction 'that's' needs an apostrophe: that is.] because they don't know where to look. By supper, I'll probably have the whole story. Mrs Atkinson might know something; she's [usualy|usually|The correct spelling is 'usually', with double l.] outside with her flowers.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: There are people who call Maycomb uneventful. I can only suppose they [spends|spend|Use the base present-tense form with 'they': they spend.] their afternoons asleep. Before breakfast, I've noticed a borrowed motorcar, an [unfamilar|unfamiliar|The correct spelling is 'unfamiliar': un-familiar.] parcel and a neighbour wearing her Sunday hat on a Tuesday. None of it [prove|proves|'None of it' refers to an uncountable amount of evidence, so use singular 'proves'.] anything, naturally. Still, I move my chair a little nearer the porch rail, where the view of the street is [considerable|considerably|Use the adverb 'considerably' to modify the comparative adjective 'better'.] better.

title: Mrs Dubose
text: From my chair, I can see the road and my roses. The [flouwers|flowers|The correct spelling is 'flowers'; there is no u.] look better than most of the children who [passes|pass|'Who' refers to the plural noun 'children', so use 'pass'.] this house. Dirty faces, loud voices, no manners. I tell them so. [An proper town|A proper town|Use 'a' before the consonant sound at the start of 'proper'.] needs people who care about [this|these|Use 'these' before the plural noun 'things'.] things. Now and then, someone stops and speaks politely. I enjoy that, though I don't always say it.

title: Mrs Dubose
text: Scrape, scrape. Another pair of [shooes|shoes|The correct spelling is 'shoes', with one o.] dragged past my gate. Does nobody [teaches|teach|After 'Does', use the base verb: Does nobody teach...?] children to lift their feet? I sit among my roses and watch Maycomb grow careless. Hats stay on when they ought to come off, and young people answer before you've finished [speak|speaking|After 'finished', use the -ing form: finished speaking.]. At least my garden still shows what attention can do. I move my chair [more further|further|'Further' is already comparative; do not add 'more'.] into the shade.

title: Mrs Dubose
text: My porch gives me a clear view of the street, though what passes for [behavour|behaviour|The correct spelling is 'behaviour': behav-iour.] there gives me little satisfaction. Children shriek; men neglect to remove their hats. I haven't spent a lifetime [learn|learning|After 'spend a lifetime', use the -ing form: learning.] proper behaviour to watch it disappear without [comment,|comment.|These are separate complete sentences; use a full stop here.] Beneath the rail, my roses hold their heads up. Their scent [reach|reaches|The head noun 'scent' is singular, so use 'reaches', even though 'Their' refers to several roses.] me whenever the air stirs, and I settle deeper into my chair.

title: Nathan Radley
text: I like our gate closed. People in Maycomb [asks|ask|'People' is plural, so use 'ask'.] too many questions, especially when a house is [qiuet|quiet|The correct spelling is 'quiet': qui-et.]. There's work to [doing|do|Use the base verb after 'to' in 'work to do'.] here, just as there is anywhere else. I clear the yard and check the fence. Beyond it, children shout and neighbours talk. I can hear them [perfect|perfectly|Use the adverb 'perfectly' to modify 'well': perfectly well.] well. That doesn't mean I need to open the door.

title: Nathan Radley
text: The [hedje|hedge|The correct spelling is 'hedge', ending in -dge.] needs cutting again. I work along it slowly, [heard|hearing|Use the -ing form to describe what I do while working: hearing footsteps.] footsteps pause on the other side. In Maycomb, a quiet household gives people something to [discussing|discuss|After 'something to', use the base verb: something to discuss.], and ours [seem|seems|'Ours' means our household here, so it takes singular 'seems'.] to interest them more than most. Let them talk. There's comfort in a straight fence and a gate that shuts properly. When I've finished outside, I put the tools away and go in.

title: Nathan Radley
text: Neighbours mistake [privacey|privacy|The correct spelling is 'privacy', ending in -acy.] for a reason to invent stories. I've lived long enough in Maycomb to recognise that habit, and I see no reason to [encouraging|encourage|Use the base verb in this to-infinitive: no reason to encourage it.] it. Along our fence, I check a loose board and press the gate against [it's|its|Use possessive 'its' for the gate's latch. 'It's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.] latch. Beyond the hedge, conversation stops for a moment. By the time it [start|starts|The subject 'it' is singular: it starts again.] again, I'm carrying my tools towards the back of the house.

title: Boo Radley
text: I hear Maycomb before I see it. [Wheels passes|Wheels pass|'Wheels' is plural, so use 'pass'.] the house, and birds sing in the trees outside. When children run along the road, [there|their|Use possessive 'their' to show whose voices they are.] voices come through the window. I listen until they are gone. At night, everything is [softter|softer|Do not double t after the consonant group -ft: softer.]. A dog moves near the fence. Leaves touch the wall. I know [much|many|Use 'many' with countable plural nouns: many sounds.] small sounds in this quiet room.

title: Boo Radley
text: Through a [narow|narrow|The correct spelling is 'narrow', with double r.] space beside the curtain, I can watch the light move across the street. Morning brings footsteps, carts and voices I [recognises|recognise|Use 'recognise' with 'I': voices I recognise.] without [see|seeing|After the preposition 'without', use the -ing form: without seeing.] their faces. Later, the heat empties the road. A bird lands on our fence and tilts its head towards the house. I stay still. For a moment, we watch [each others|each other|The reciprocal expression is 'each other', without a final s.] through the dusty glass.

title: Boo Radley
text: The town reaches my room in [pieces;|pieces:|Use a colon to introduce the descriptive list; a semicolon does not introduce this list of phrases.] a wheel striking a stone, kitchen smoke drifting through a gap, laughter passing and fading. I put these [fragmants|fragments|The correct spelling is 'fragments', ending in -ments.] together until I can almost follow the street beyond my window. Towards evening, shadows join beneath the trees. [Less|Fewer|Use 'fewer' with countable plural nouns: fewer eyes.] eyes outside then. I stand a little closer to the glass and watch a small moth [settles|settle|After 'watch' plus an object, use the base form or an -ing form: watch a moth settle, not settles.] there.

title: Dill
text: Every [houses|house|After 'Every', use a singular noun: every house.] in Maycomb looks like the start of a story. A dark window? There could [is|be|After 'could', use the base form 'be'.] a secret room behind it. A [brokken|broken|The correct spelling is 'broken', with one k.] gate? Perhaps someone escaped last night. I like to walk slowly and look at everything. The other children know these streets already, but I keep [find|finding|After 'keep', use an -ing form: keep finding.] new things. Even a strange noise can give me an idea.

title: Dill
text: Maycomb's got enough stories for a hundred summers, if you ask me. I can turn a [croocked|crooked|The correct spelling is 'crooked', with one c.] tree into a giant and a locked shed into a [pirates|pirate's|Use apostrophe-s to show that the store belongs to a pirate.] store. The others say I'm [make|making|After 'I'm' in this continuous form, use 'making'.] things up. Well, of course I am! By evening, when the porches glow and [families calls|families call|'Families' is plural, so use 'call'.] their children home, I sometimes wish I belonged to one of those pictures.

title: Dill
text: Summer makes a stage of [Maycomb,|Maycomb.|Separate these complete sentences with a full stop.] Behind every curtain, I imagine a secret; down every lane, an adventure waiting for [it's|its|Use possessive 'its' for the adventure's leading man; 'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.] leading man. Naturally, I volunteer. The town is generous with [scenary|scenery|The correct spelling is 'scenery', ending in -ery.]: leaning fences, mysterious gardens, sheds that deserve investigation. Then a mother calls from a doorway, and the other children drift home. I linger beneath the trees, rehearsing something splendid to [tells|tell|Use the base verb in 'to tell them', not the third-person form.] them tomorrow.

title: Heck Tate
text: Most mornings, I walk around the square and speak to the [shopkeppers|shopkeepers|The correct spelling is 'shopkeepers', with double e.]. They [tells|tell|Use 'tell' with 'they': they tell me.] me about broken windows, missing things and dogs that won't stay home. I listen. Usually, the town is [quietly|quiet|Use an adjective after 'is' to describe the town: the town is quiet.], but I still look down the side streets. By evening, I know which [shops is|shops are|'Shops' is plural, so use 'are'.] closed and which lights are burning. It's part of being the sheriff.

title: Heck Tate
text: From a distance, Maycomb looks [peacful|peaceful|Keep the final e of 'peace' when adding -ful: peaceful.] enough: wagons by the stores, men exchanging news, children under [everybodys|everybody's|Use possessive apostrophe-s: everybody's feet.] feet. I know which voices to [listen at|listen for|Use 'listen for' when trying to notice a particular sound or voice.]. A sudden shout can mean nothing; [two man|two men|The irregular plural of 'man' is 'men': two men.] speaking too quietly may need watching. Mostly, though, my rounds bring ordinary complaints. I stop outside a shop, adjust my hat and hear about another broken fence.

title: Heck Tate
text: A sheriff learns to read the square by [it's|its|Use possessive 'its' for the square's disturbances; 'it's' is a contraction.] small [disturbences|disturbances|The correct spelling is 'disturbances', ending in -ances.]. One shop opening late; a horse left restless at the rail; conversation stopping as I approach. Most mean nothing serious, but I notice them all the same. Under the awnings, men debate weather and money while wagons [grinds|grind|The subject 'wagons' is plural, so use 'grind'.] past. I exchange a greeting, pause for an answer, then [continuing|continue|Keep the coordinated verbs parallel: I exchange, pause, then continue.] towards the next doorway.

title: Judge Taylor
text: The [courthous|courthouse|The correct spelling is 'courthouse', including the final e.] is a good place to watch Maycomb. From a window, I can see people [crosses|crossing|After 'see people', use the base form or -ing form: see people crossing.] the square with bags and baskets. Their voices rise through the warm air. Inside, papers wait on my desk. I take off my glasses and rub my [eye's|eyes|Use the plural 'eyes', without an apostrophe.]. Outside, a man stops to talk. [Him|His|Use the possessive 'His' before the noun 'horse'.] horse must wait, and so must my work.

title: Judge Taylor
text: By mid-afternoon, the heat has [setled|settled|The correct spelling is 'settled', with double t.] over the courthouse like [an thick blanket|a thick blanket|Use 'a' before the consonant sound in 'thick'.]. I loosen my collar and listen to a fly [quarrelling to|quarrelling with|The usual construction is 'quarrel with' someone or something.] the window. Down below, Maycomb carries on at its usual pace. A wagon rolls past; two neighbours begin a conversation neither seems likely to finish. The papers on my desk haven't [move|moved|After 'haven't', use the past participle: haven't moved.] either. I reach for my glasses.

title: Judge Taylor
text: Official business has [it's|its|Use possessive 'its' to show that the hours belong to official business.] hours; Maycomb has its own [arrangments|arrangements|The correct spelling is 'arrangements': arrange-ments.]. From my courthouse window, I watch a man abandon an errand for a conversation that could [comfortable|comfortably|Use an adverb to modify 'outlast': comfortably outlast.] outlast both. Heat gathers beneath the roof, and a fly conducts an energetic inspection of my desk. I remove my glasses, rub the bridge of my nose, and [allowing|allow|Keep the main verbs parallel: I remove, rub, and allow.] the town another minute before returning to its paperwork.

title: Reverend Sykes
text: On [Sonday|Sunday|The correct spelling is 'Sunday'.] mornings, I hear people coming towards our church. Some walk a long way, and their shoes [is|are|'Their shoes' is plural, so use 'are'.] covered in dust. We open the doors to [lets|let|After 'to', use the base verb: to let in the air.] in the air. Soon the room is full of faces I know. I see tired people smiling at their friends. When we sing, the sound grows strong enough to fill every quiet [corners|corner|After 'every', use a singular noun: every corner.].

title: Reverend Sykes
text: Our church stands beyond the [comfortible|comfortable|The correct spelling is 'comfortable': comfort-able.] streets that visitors usually admire. I know the families who walk here, carrying a [weeks|week's|Use the possessive apostrophe in 'a week's tiredness'.] tiredness in their shoulders. Before the service, we share news of work, illness and children. Someone always [need|needs|'Someone' takes a singular verb: someone needs help.] help, and someone usually has a little to give. Then the singing begins. Beside the open door, I hear the whole room [to breathe|breathe|After 'hear' plus an object, use the base form or an -ing form without 'to': hear the room breathe.] together.

title: Reverend Sykes
text: Long before I begin the service, the [congregration|congregation|The correct spelling is 'congregation', without an extra r after g.] tells me how well Maycomb is managing. An empty seat, a worried glance, a quiet question about work: each [ask|asks|The subject 'each' is singular, so use 'asks'.] for [attention,|attention.|Use a full stop between these complete sentences.] Outside, dust whitens the shoes of late arrivals. Inside, neighbours make room along the benches. When the singing rises, I hear familiar voices supporting one another, the uncertain ones [gradual|gradually|Use the adverb 'gradually' to modify 'finding'.] finding their strength among the rest.

title: Helen Robinson
text: I like the time just before supper, when our neighbours come outside. [Children plays|Children play|'Children' is plural, so use 'play'.] near the houses, and women call across the road. I can [puts|put|After 'can', use the base verb: can put.] down my work for a few [minites|minutes|The correct spelling is 'minutes'.]. There are worries, of course, but [there are laughter|there is laughter|'Laughter' is uncountable, so use singular 'there is'.] too. A friend asks how I am, and I tell her. In our part of Maycomb, that matters.

title: Helen Robinson
text: My children can [found|find|After 'can', use the base verb: can find.] a game in almost [anyting|anything|The correct spelling is 'anything', including h.]: a stick, an empty box, a patch of shade. I watch them while I finish the washing. Beyond our houses, Maycomb has gardens and shop windows that [seems|seem|'That' refers to the plural 'gardens and shop windows', so use 'seem'.] to belong to another world. Here, a neighbour calls out an offer of help. I smile back, then spread another damp shirt [among|between|The shirt is held between the speaker's two hands; use 'between' for this position.] my hands.

title: Helen Robinson
text: There are afternoons when Maycomb seems to measure out its [comfort's|comforts|Use the plural 'comforts', without an apostrophe.] street by street. Beyond our [neigbourhood|neighbourhood|The correct spelling is 'neighbourhood', including h after g.], gardens are [planting|planted|The gardens receive the action, so use the passive: are planted.] for pleasure; here, every scrap of ground must earn its keep. Yet warmth travels easily between our [doorways,|doorways.|Separate these complete sentences with a full stop.] A neighbour watches the children while I finish a chore. Later, I carry over something from our kitchen and stay to talk as the light fades.

title: Mayella Ewell
text: Town looks [prety|pretty|The correct spelling is 'pretty', with double t.] from [an long way|a long way|Use 'a' before the consonant sound at the start of 'long'.] off. I can see trees around the houses, and I think about the clean rooms inside. Near our place, there's rubbish beside the road. The little children make a lot of noise. I try to [grows|grow|After 'try to', use the base verb: try to grow.] a few flowers because I like looking at something nice. [There|Their|Use possessive 'Their' to show that the heads belong to the flowers.] bright heads turn towards the sun.

title: Mayella Ewell
text: [Sometims|Sometimes|The correct spelling is 'Sometimes', including e before the final s.] I look towards town and imagine a house where every chair [have|has|'Every chair' is singular, so use 'has'.] its own place. There'd [is|be|After 'would', including the contraction 'there'd', use the base form 'be'.] clean curtains, perhaps, and nobody stepping over things on the floor. Here, the children shout and the smell of rubbish hangs in the heat. I water my flowers carefully. They're small, but [they're|their|Use possessive 'their' for the flowers' colour. 'They're' means 'they are'.] colour catches my eye whenever I come through the yard.

title: Mayella Ewell
text: From our end of the road, Maycomb's [respectible|respectable|The correct spelling is 'respectable', ending in -able.] houses seem impossibly complete: fences without gaps, curtains that [matches|match|'That' refers to the plural noun 'curtains', so use 'match'.], front steps someone has time to scrub. I wonder what it feels like to open a door without [want|wanting|After the preposition 'without', use the -ing form: without wanting.] to hide what's [behind its|behind it|After the preposition 'behind', use the object pronoun 'it'; 'its' is possessive.]. Rubbish shifts in the ditch outside our yard. I turn towards my flowers, touching a leaf to see whether they need water.

title: Bob Ewell
text: Those men in town like to stand outside the shops and look [importent|important|The correct spelling is 'important', ending in -ant.]. I know what [them think|they think|Use the subject pronoun 'they' before the verb 'think'.] when I walk past. Let them look. Their houses might be [more bigger|bigger|'Bigger' is already comparative; do not add 'more'.] than mine, but they don't [owns|own|After 'don't', use the base verb: don't own.] every road in Maycomb. I go where I please. At our end of town, there's room to spit without somebody telling you how to behave.

title: Bob Ewell
text: There's a certain way the shopkeepers watch [an man|a man|Use 'a' before the consonant sound at the start of 'man'.] when his clothes aren't good enough for them. I've seen it often. They stand behind their [counnters|counters|The correct spelling is 'counters', with one n.] as if a clean shirt [make|makes|The subject 'a clean shirt' is singular, so use 'makes'.] them kings. Well, I won't [bowed|bow|After 'won't', use the base verb: won't bow.] to the lot of them. Out by our place, dogs nose through rubbish and children kick up dust. Nobody there tells me where to stand.

title: Bob Ewell
text: Fine houses, [pollished|polished|The correct spelling is 'polished', with one l.] shoes, neighbours forever [judgement|judging|Use the -ing form before the object 'a man's fence'; 'judgement' is a noun.] a [mans|man's|Use possessive apostrophe-s to show whose fence it is: a man's fence.] fence. That's Maycomb for you. Walk into a store without money and watch the welcome cool. I know I'm poor; I still expect the respect due a white man. Beyond the neat streets, rubbish smokes beside the road to our place. I kick a bottle out of my path and leave it where it [land|lands|Use singular 'lands' with 'it' in the clause 'where it lands'.].

title: Mr Gilmer
text: When work brings me to Maycomb, I go straight to the square. The courthouse is easy to find, and most of the [shops is|shops are|'Shops' is plural, so use 'are'.] nearby. People stop to talk more [then|than|Use 'than' in a comparison: more than I would like.] I would [likes|like|After 'would', use the base verb: would like.]. I prefer to finish my [buisness|business|The correct spelling is 'business': bus-i-ness.] first. Still, I notice who says hello and who looks away. A small town can tell you quite a lot.

title: Mr Gilmer
text: Maycomb always seems to have time for another [converstation|conversation|The correct spelling is 'conversation'; do not add t after s.]. I arrive with papers to [sorted|sort|After 'to', use the base verb: papers to sort.], yet somebody wants to discuss a neighbour's family before I've [took|taken|After 'I've', use the past participle 'taken', not the simple past 'took'.] off my hat. Names [matters|matter|The subject 'Names' is plural, so use 'matter'.] here, perhaps more than they should. I listen all the same. By the time I reach the courthouse, I've learnt who owns the store, who owes money and who expects attention.

title: Mr Gilmer
text: For a visiting lawyer, Maycomb requires a certain amount of listening before any useful business begins. Family [connetions|connections|The correct spelling is 'connections', including c before t.] are explained, old disagreements revived, introductions prolonged. I keep my [impatient|impatience|After possessive 'my', this position needs a noun: my impatience.] behind a polite expression. Around the square, influence announces itself quietly: a shopkeeper leaving his counter to greet one customer, barely looking up at another. Such distinctions are worth [remember|remembering|After 'worth', use the -ing form: worth remembering.] when one [work|works|The generic pronoun 'one' takes a singular verb: one works.] here.

title: Tom Robinson
text: [Eerly|Early|The correct spelling is 'Early', beginning with Ear-.] in the morning, I walk past the fields while the air is still cool. Birds [moves|move|'Birds' is plural, so use 'move'.] in the long grass, and I can [smells|smell|After 'can', use the base verb: can smell.] the earth. Later, town gets busy. I speak politely and keep out of people's way. At home, the children run to meet me. Their voices are the sound I like [most best|best|'Best' is already superlative; do not add 'most'.] in all of Maycomb.

title: Tom Robinson
text: I know the roads around Maycomb by the dust they leave on [mine boots|my boots|Use 'my' before the noun 'boots'; 'mine' stands alone.]. Work takes me past fields, fences and houses where I wouldn't [been|be|After 'wouldn't', use the base form 'be', not the participle 'been'.] [welcom|welcome|The correct spelling is 'welcome', including the final e.] inside. I watch my step and mind my words. Near home, I can walk a little easier. Someone's cooking, children are laughing, and Helen lifts her face when she [hearing|hears|This time clause needs a finite verb: when she hears me.] me at the door.

title: Tom Robinson
text: Dawn gives the roads a brief [gentelness|gentleness|The correct spelling is 'gentleness': gentle-ness.]. I walk towards work while mist hangs over the fields, before the heat and the watching eyes [gathers|gather|The compound subject 'the heat and the watching eyes' is plural, so use 'gather'.]. In town, I pay [attention at|attention to|The construction is 'pay attention to' something, not 'pay attention at'.] how close I stand and how quickly I answer. Those habits follow me home, but loosen there. Hearing the children call, I lift my good hand in greeting and [lengthening|lengthen|Keep the coordinated main verbs parallel: I lift my hand and lengthen my stride.] my stride.

title: Mr Cunningham
text: I come into Maycomb when there's something I [needs|need|Use the base present-tense form with 'I': I need.] for the farm. The shops have plenty of [thing|things|After 'plenty of', use the plural countable noun 'things' here.] I can't buy, so I don't [spent|spend|After 'don't', use the base verb: don't spend.] long looking. A bag of seed matters more than a new coat. Once my business is done, I'm glad to leave. Out beyond the houses, I can watch the sky and think about the [wheather|weather|The correct spelling is 'weather', without an extra h after w.].

title: Mr Cunningham
text: The square [smell|smells|The subject 'The square' is singular, so use 'smells'.] of horses, hot dust and things for sale. I bring my list, count my money and try to [kept|keep|After 'try to', use the base verb: try to keep.] the two in [agrement|agreement|The correct spelling is 'agreement', with double e.]. Nobody needs to tell me times are hard. You can see it in the farmers' patched coats. Once I've bought what I can, I head home. There's a field waiting that won't care how [me look|I look|Use the subject pronoun 'I' before 'look'; 'me' is an object pronoun.].

title: Mr Cunningham
text: Before setting out for Maycomb, I work out what the farm can [aford|afford|The correct spelling is 'afford', with double f.]. The answer rarely fills a shopping bag. Around the square, other men make similar calculations, turning a tool over before [ask|asking|After the preposition 'before', use the -ing form: before asking.] its price. We discuss rain instead of money; [its|it's|Here the meaning is 'it is easier', so the contraction needs an apostrophe: it's.] easier. By late afternoon, I welcome the road home, where the smell of worked earth [replace|replaces|The subject is singular 'the smell of worked earth', so use 'replaces'.] the dust of the stores.
